summary: Portugal is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorisation being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90. Long-stay options include the D7 passive-income visa and the D8 digital nomad visa.

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since 11 June 2024.
For stays over 90 days: work, study, family reunification and other residence purposes. Fee varies slightly by consulate and purpose.
For retirees and holders of passive income (pensions, rents, dividends) of at least the Portuguese minimum wage (around €870/month, updated annually).
For remote workers employed by non-Portuguese companies; income requirement of four times the Portuguese minimum wage (roughly €3,480/month, updated annually).
Required for courses longer than 90 days; needs proof of enrolment, funds and health insurance.
Requires an employment contract or promise of employment in Portugal before the visa application.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Portugal sets a minimum means requirement for non-EU visitors: €75 per entry plus €40 per person per day. Officers rarely check, but can ask at the border.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards, contactless and the local MB Way app are accepted almost everywhere. Some small cafés, taxis and rural shops still prefer cash.

safety.text: Portugal consistently ranks among the safest countries in the world. The main visitor risk is pickpocketing in Lisbon and Porto, especially on trams and at viewpoints.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Portugal Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October bring warm, dry weather without the August crowds; the Algarve stays mild even in winter.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Portugal — days spent in Spain or France count against the same allowance.
Watch valuables on Lisbon's tram 28 and at crowded miradouros — pickpocketing is the most common tourist crime.
Several Portuguese motorways use electronic-only tolls with no cash booths — rent a transponder with your hire car or register your plate online before driving.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Portugal?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Portugal and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorisation (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Portugal Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: What income do I need for the Portugal D7 visa?
faq.answer: The D7 requires stable passive income (pension, rents, dividends) of at least the Portuguese minimum wage — around €870 per month, updated annually. The visa fee is about €90 and the visa leads to a residence permit.

faq.question: Does Portugal have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Yes. The D8 visa is for remote workers employed by companies outside Portugal. You must show average monthly income of four times the Portuguese minimum wage — roughly €3,480 per month — over the last three months. The visa fee is about €90.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Portugal without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
